# Reviewer Comment 1 - Data collection, train/test procedure, confidence intervals and accuracy percentages

## 1.1 Data collection
Each onboard sensor was operated side-by-side with a reference instrument, and both were logged simultaneously at a fixed interval (10 s for the NFADS and EMS nodes, 40 s for the LMS node), giving time-stamped paired readings (sensor_i, reference_i). Four independent single-session experiments were performed (Table 1): TDS (42 pairs, 6.8 min, reference ranging from 350 to 944 PPM), air temperature in the EMS node (53 pairs, 8.7 min), nutrient temperature in the NFADS node (62 pairs, 10.2 min) and light intensity in the LMS node (753 pairs over 8.4 h, 08:50:10-17:11:30, reference range 0-20054 lux). | TDS (NFADS) | TDS Sensor vs. TDS Meter | 13:10:45-13:17:35 | 6.8 min | 42 | 10 s | 350-944 (SD 179) |

## 1.2 Train/test (validation) procedure
The OLS calibration `reference = a * sensor + b` was originally fitted and scored on the same pairs (resubstitution). Such in-sample figures are optimistic, so all accuracy figures were re-computed with time-ordered validation, which is appropriate because consecutive samples are strongly autocorrelated (residual lag-1 autocorrelation 0.52-0.86):

1. **Blocked 5-fold cross-validation (primary).** Each record was cut into five contiguous time blocks without shuffling; every block was predicted by a calibration line fitted only on the other four blocks, and RMSE, MAE, bias and R² were computed on the pooled out-of-fold predictions. Fold sizes were 9/11/151 samples (TDS/EMS/Lux).
2. **Chronological 70/30 hold-out (secondary).** The first 70 % of the record trained the line and the last 30 % tested it (TDS 29/13, EMS 37/16, Lux 527/226).
3. **Leave-one-out** is reported only as a contrast: it leaks information between neighbouring samples and under-estimates the error (TDS RMSE 24.3 vs. 40.1 PPM with blocked CV).

**Table 2. Out-of-sample error of the same OLS model under different protocols** (RMSE in sensor units; accuracy % in brackets; chronological hold-out is scored on its own test segment).

| Quantity | In-sample (fit = test) | Blocked 5-fold CV (out-of-fold) | Chronological 70/30 hold-out | Leave-one-out (leaky) | R² in-sample | R² out-of-fold |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TDS [PPM] | 23.2 (96.3 %) | 40.1 (93.6 %) | 45.9 (94.7 %) | 24.3 (96.1 %) | 0.983 | 0.950 |
| Air temp. [°C] | 0.0535 (99.8 %) | 0.0704 (99.8 %) | 0.0486 (99.8 %) | 0.0555 (99.8 %) | 0.485 | 0.108 |
| Light [Lux] | 120 (98.5 %) | 151 (98.1 %) | 129 (97.0 %) | 120 (98.5 %) | 1.000 | 0.999 |

Out-of-sample error was higher than the in-sample error for every sensor (TDS 23.2 -> 40.1 PPM, EMS 0.054 -> 0.070 °C, Lux 120 -> 151 lux), so the in-sample values are reported only for reference. For the EMS 30 % hold-out segment the reference was constant, so R² is undefined there (n/a).

## 1.3 Confidence intervals
* **Slope and intercept.** The original intervals were classical Student-t intervals, estimate ± t(0.975, n-2) * SE, with SE(intercept) = SE(slope) * sqrt(sum(x²)/n). They assume independent residuals, which does not hold here (Durbin-Watson 0.28-0.96; effective sample size n_eff = n(1-ρ)/(1+ρ) is only 9 of 42, 17 of 53, 58 of 753 for TDS, EMS, Lux). We therefore also report **moving-block bootstrap** 95 % intervals (B = 2000, paired blocks of length b = ceil(2n/n_eff) = 10, 7, 26 samples, 2.5th-97.5th percentiles). The classical slope intervals were too narrow by a factor of 2.2-4.8; the block-bootstrap intervals are the ones that should be quoted (Table 3, Figure R2).
* **"Calibration interval" ±1.96·RMSE.** This is *not* a confidence interval for a parameter. It is a 95 % reading-uncertainty band for a single calibrated reading, assuming approximately normal, zero-mean errors. We now compute it from the out-of-fold RMSE; its empirical out-of-fold coverage was 95-98 %, confirming that it is adequate (slightly conservative).
* **Uncertainty of RMSE / accuracy %.** The 95 % CI of the out-of-fold RMSE was obtained by block-bootstrapping the out-of-fold squared errors (same b, B = 2000) and transformed to accuracy % through the accuracy formula below.

**Table 3. Calibration parameters with classical vs. autocorrelation-aware 95 % intervals.**

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TDS | 0.66 | 42 / 9 | [0.8442, 0.9177] | [0.6599, 1.0120] | [27.732, 77.975] | [-23.007, 176.221] |
| Air temp. | 0.52 | 53 / 17 | [0.6545, 1.1885] | [0.1356, 1.2887] | [-5.535, 10.646] | [-8.592, 26.386] |

## 1.4 Accuracy percentages
Accuracy (%) = 100 * (1 - RMSE / mean(reference)), where the RMSE is the out-of-fold RMSE and the mean is that of the reference meter over the test. Because this ratio is dominated by the mean, it is nearly 100 % for temperature (mean ≈ 30 °C) even when the sensor barely follows the reference. We therefore also give the span-normalised accuracy 100 * (1 - RMSE / (max - min of reference)) and the absolute error in measurement units (Table 4).

**Table 4. Accuracy summary (headline = out-of-fold).**

| Quantity | Raw accuracy % | In-sample accuracy % (original) | Out-of-fold accuracy % (95% CI) | Out-of-fold span-accuracy % | Out-of-fold RMSE | Reading band ±1.96·RMSE |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TDS | 93.4 | 96.3 | 93.6 [92.20–96.71] | 93.3 | 40.1 PPM | ±78.6 PPM |
| Air temp. | 99.4 | 99.8 | 99.8 [99.72–99.80] | 64.8 | 0.0704 °C | ±0.138 °C |
| Light | 66.1 | 98.5 | 98.1 [97.87–98.34] | 99.2 | 151 Lux | ±295 Lux |

For the nutrient-temperature test the reference meter stayed at a constant 30.8 °C, so slope and intercept cannot be estimated and R² is undefined; the earlier "±0.00 °C after OLS" is a degenerate fit and has been withdrawn. The test is reported only as a fixed offset: the sensor read -0.68 °C relative to the meter (95 % CI ±0.007 °C, n = 62; sensor SD 0.029 °C; MAE 0.68 °C).

## 1.5 Limitations (to be stated in the paper)
Each calibration comes from one session with one unit; three of the four records last under 11 minutes, and the EMS reference spans only 0.2 °C at 0.1 °C resolution, so the temperature response cannot be characterised. The lux reference (TSL2591) is itself a sensor, not a calibrated lux meter. The reported intervals therefore describe the repeatability of these specific sessions; multi-day, multi-unit validation over a wider range is required before claiming general accuracy.

# Reviewer Comment 2 - Why the pre-calibration air-temperature R² is negative

## 2.1 Explanation (paper-ready)
The negative value (raw R² = -5.18, EMS air temperature) is a property of the metric, not a computational error. R² = 1 - SSE/SST compares the sensor with a trivial baseline that always outputs the mean of the reference; it is negative whenever the sensor's squared error SSE exceeds the squared spread SST of the reference around its own mean. In the EMS test the reference stayed within 30.4-30.6 °C (SD = 0.075 °C, SST = 0.295 °C²), whereas the uncalibrated sensor read a nearly constant 0.177 °C *below* the reference (SSE = 1.820 °C²). Hence SSE/SST = 6.18 and R² = 1 - 6.18 = -5.18.

The result follows exactly from the identity

R² = r² - (r - s_sensor/s_ref)² - (bias/s_ref)²,

where r is the Pearson correlation, s the standard deviations and bias = mean(sensor) - mean(reference). For the EMS data: r² = 0.485 (correlation is positive), scale-mismatch term = 0.004 (negligible, s_sensor/s_ref = 0.76), bias term = (-0.177/0.075)² = 5.66, which accounts for 92 % of the mean-square error. Because r² ≤ 1, R² ≤ 1 - (bias/s_ref)²: **any offset larger than the spread of the reference makes R² negative, however small the offset is in absolute terms** (Figure R3c). TDS and light do not show this because their reference spread (SD 179 PPM, 5727 lux) is large relative to their bias (|bias|/SD = 0.14 and 0.39 versus 2.38 for air temperature), so their raw R² stays positive (0.946, 0.784) (Table 5).

**Table 5. Decomposition of raw R² (R² = r² − scale − bias).**

| Quantity | Reference SD | Sensor bias | |bias| / ref. SD | SSE / SST | r² (+) | scale (−) | bias (−) | Raw R² |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TDS | 179 PPM | +24.81 PPM | 0.14 | 0.054 | 0.983 | 0.018 | 0.019 | 0.946 |
| Light | 5727 Lux | +2208 Lux | 0.39 | 0.216 | 1.000 | 0.067 | 0.149 | 0.784 |
| Air temp. | 0.07457 °C | -0.1774 °C | 2.38 | 6.175 | 0.485 | 0.004 | 5.657 | -5.175 |

## 2.2 What this does and does not say about the sensor
* **The offset is physically small.** The raw RMSE is 0.19 °C and the bias -0.18 °C (0.58 % of the reading). The Bland-Altman 95 % limits of agreement for the raw sensor are [-0.28, -0.07] °C. The sensor is *consistently low*, not noisy: the SD of the difference is only 0.054 °C.
* **The "improvement" after calibration is almost entirely offset removal.** OLS forces the mean error to zero, so the in-sample R² becomes r² = 0.485 (from -5.18) while the correlation itself is unchanged (r = 0.696). The in-sample value is optimistic: out-of-fold R² is 0.11.
* **The modest correlation is largely a resolution effect.** Both devices log in 0.1 °C steps (only 3 distinct reference values over a 0.2 °C span). Rounding noise (SD ≈ 0.029 °C, q/√12) equals about 15 % of the reference variance and 26 % of the sensor variance, which caps the attainable correlation at about r ≈ 0.79 (R² ≈ 0.63) even for a perfect sensor.
* **R² is therefore the wrong headline metric for this test.** With the same absolute error (MSE = 0.0343 °C²) R² would exceed 0.99 if the reference SD were 2 °C (a wider temperature sweep), and would be 0 at an SD of only 0.19 °C.

## 2.3 Recommended wording for the manuscript
> Prior to calibration, the EMS air-temperature sensor showed a negative coefficient of determination (R² = -5.18). This is a consequence of the narrow reference range during the test (30.4-30.6 °C, SD = 0.075 °C) combined with a systematic offset of -0.18 °C: R² benchmarks the sensor against the reference mean, and the squared offset (0.0315 °C²) was 5.7 times the reference variance (0.0056 °C²). The sensor tracked the reference direction (r = 0.70) with low scatter (SD of differences 0.054 °C), and OLS calibration removed the offset (bias -0.18 → 0 °C; RMSE 0.185 → 0.054 °C in-sample, 0.070 °C out-of-fold). For near-constant temperature we therefore report bias, MAE, RMSE and Bland-Altman limits of agreement rather than R², and we note that the R² of 0.48 after calibration (out-of-fold 0.11) is limited by the 0.1 °C resolution and 0.2 °C span of the test; validation over a wider temperature range is left for future work.
